characters.summary: 水 (shuǐ) is the Chinese character for water. It is written with 4 strokes and pronounced shuǐ in the third tone. It began as a picture of flowing water, and you will meet it in everyday words such as 喝水 (drink water) and 水果 (fruit).
origin: 水 is a pictograph. The oldest forms, carved on oracle bones more than 3,000 years ago, show a curving line with short marks on each side. This is traditionally explained as a picture of flowing water.
Over time the curving line straightened into the hooked vertical stroke in the middle, and the marks beside it became the strokes on the left and right.
characters.memory_aid: Think of the middle stroke as the main current and the strokes on each side as smaller streams splashing off it. This is how the video draws it. It is a way to remember the shape, not a documented stroke-by-stroke history.
characters.stroke_order: Write the hooked vertical stroke in the middle first, then the stroke on the left, then the two strokes on the right.
notes: On the left side of another character, 水 is squeezed into three short strokes: 氵. Learners often call it "three drops of water". You can see it in 河 (hé, river), 海 (hǎi, sea) and 洗 (xǐ, to wash).

quiz.explain: 水 means water.
水 is shuǐ, third tone.

quiz.q: How many strokes does 水 have?
quiz.explain: 水 has 4 strokes. The hooked vertical stroke in the middle comes first.

quiz.q: What does 喝水 (hē shuǐ) mean?
quiz.explain: 喝 is to drink, so 喝水 is to drink water.

quiz.q: Which shape is the form of 水 used on the left side of characters such as 河 (river)?
quiz.explain: 氵 is the three-stroke form of 水 that appears on the left of many water-related characters.

characters.summary: 山 (shān) is the Chinese character for mountain or hill. It is written with 3 strokes and pronounced shān in the first tone, high and level. It is a drawing of mountain peaks, and it appears in words such as 火山 (volcano) and 爬山 (to go hiking).
origin: 山 is a pictograph of mountain peaks. In oracle-bone writing, more than 3,000 years ago, the peaks were drawn as triangle-like shapes standing on a ground line rather than as upright strokes.
Over the centuries each peak thinned into a single vertical stroke, with the middle one tallest, and the ground became the line along the bottom.
characters.stroke_order: Write the tall vertical stroke in the middle first. The second stroke goes down the left side and turns along the bottom in one movement. The short vertical stroke on the right comes last.
notes: 山 is also a building block in other characters. For example, 岩 (yán, rock) is written with 山 above 石 (stone), and 岛 (dǎo, island) has 山 at the bottom.

words.en: to climb a mountain, to go hiking

quiz.explain: 山 means mountain or hill.
山 is shān, first tone: high and level.

quiz.q: How many strokes does 山 have?
quiz.explain: 山 has 3 strokes. The tall middle stroke comes first.

quiz.q: 火山 (huǒshān) is literally "fire mountain". What does it mean?
quiz.explain: 火 (fire) + 山 (mountain) = volcano.

quiz.q: In the oldest writing, how were the peaks of 山 drawn?
quiz.explain: In oracle-bone script the peaks were triangle-like shapes, not upright strokes.

characters.summary: 日 (rì) is the Chinese character for sun, and it also means day. It is written with 4 strokes and pronounced rì in the fourth tone, falling. It began as a picture of the sun, and it appears in words such as 生日 (birthday) and 日本 (Japan).
origin: 日 is a pictograph of the sun. Early forms show an outline with a dot or a short line in the middle. In today's script, written with straight strokes, the outline is a tall box and the mark is the line across the centre.
Why the mark is there is not certain. One common explanation is that it was added to tell the sun apart from other, similar-looking shapes.
The meaning "day" grew out of the meaning "sun".
characters.stroke_order: Write the left vertical stroke first. The second stroke runs across the top and down the right side in one movement. Then write the line in the middle, and close the box with the bottom line last.
notes: Look-alikes: 日 (sun) is tall and narrow with one line inside. 目 (mù, eye) has two lines inside. 曰 (yuē, an old word for "to say") is wider and flatter.
In everyday speech the usual word for the sun is 太阳 (tàiyáng) and the usual word for a day is 天 (tiān). 日 is mostly found inside words and in written dates.

quiz.q: Which two meanings does 日 have?
quiz.explain: 日 means sun, and also day.
日 is rì, fourth tone: falling.

quiz.q: How many strokes does 日 have?
quiz.explain: 日 has 4 strokes. The bottom line that closes the box comes last.
生 (birth) + 日 (day) = birthday.

quiz.q: Which of these characters is 日 (sun)?
quiz.explain: 日 has one line inside the box. 目 (eye) has two, 口 (mouth) has none, and 白 (white) has an extra stroke on top.

characters.summary: 木 (mù) is the Chinese character for tree and for wood. It is written with 4 strokes and pronounced mù in the fourth tone, falling. It began as a picture of a tree with branches above and roots below, and it appears in words such as 木头 (wood) and 树木 (trees).
origin: 木 is a pictograph of a tree. Early forms show a trunk with branches reaching up at the top and roots spreading out at the bottom.
characters.memory_aid: In the video the trunk is the vertical stroke, the branches flatten into the line across, and the roots become the two sweeping strokes. That is how the shapes line up when you put the old form next to the modern one. Treat it as a way to remember the character rather than a documented stroke-by-stroke history.
characters.stroke_order: Write the horizontal stroke first, then the vertical stroke through it, then the sweeping stroke to the left, and the sweeping stroke to the right last.
notes: In modern Chinese the everyday word for a tree is 树 (shù). On its own, 木 usually refers to wood.

木 is a building block in many characters to do with trees and wooden things, such as 桌 (zhuō, table) and 椅 (yǐ, chair). 林 (lín, woods) is traditionally explained as two trees side by side, and 森 (sēn, as in 森林, forest) as three.

quiz.explain: 木 means tree, and also wood.
木 is mù, fourth tone: falling.

quiz.q: How many strokes does 木 have?
quiz.explain: 木 has 4 strokes. The horizontal stroke comes first.
木头 is wood, the material.

quiz.q: 林 is written with two 木 side by side. What does it mean?
quiz.explain: 林 (lín) means woods. It is traditionally explained as two trees standing together.

characters.summary: 火 (huǒ) is the Chinese character for fire. It is written with 4 strokes and pronounced huǒ in the third tone. It began as a picture of flames, and it appears in words such as 火车 (train, literally "fire vehicle") and 火山 (volcano).
origin: 火 is a pictograph of fire. The oracle-bone form shown on this page, more than 3,000 years old, is a flame shape with points rising from a base.
The modern character keeps the idea of flames reaching upward, but its four strokes do not match the parts of the old drawing one for one.
characters.memory_aid: Think of the two long strokes as a tall flame and the two short strokes as sparks flying off on each side. This is how the video draws it. It is a memory aid only and is not how the old form was laid out.
characters.stroke_order: Write the two short strokes first, left and then right. Then write the long sweeping stroke to the left, and the long sweeping stroke to the right last.
notes: At the bottom of another character, 火 is often written as four dots: 灬. You can see it in 热 (rè, hot) and 点 (diǎn, dot; to light). On the left side it keeps its shape but gets narrower, as in 灯 (dēng, lamp) and 烧 (shāo, to burn).

quiz.explain: 火 means fire.
火 is huǒ, third tone.

quiz.q: How many strokes does 火 have?
quiz.explain: 火 has 4 strokes.

quiz.q: 火车 (huǒchē) is literally "fire vehicle". What does it mean?
quiz.explain: 火车 is a train. The name comes from steam locomotives.

quiz.q: Which strokes of 火 are written first?
options: The long stroke on the right
The long stroke on the left
quiz.explain: The two short strokes come first, left then right, followed by the two long strokes.

characters.summary: 人 (rén) is the Chinese character for person. It is written with 2 strokes and pronounced rén in the second tone. It began as a side view of a standing person, and you will meet it in everyday words such as 大人 (adult) and 人口 (population).
origin: 人 is a pictograph. The oldest forms, on oracle bones more than 3,000 years ago, show a standing person seen from the side, drawn with a few lines that pick out an arm and a leg.
The modern character keeps just two strokes of that figure.
characters.memory_aid: Think of the two strokes as a person walking: the body and one leg, then the other leg. This is how the video draws it. It is a way to remember the shape, not a stroke-by-stroke history.
characters.stroke_order: Two strokes: first the stroke that falls to the left, then the stroke that falls to the right, starting from the middle of the first one.
notes: On the left side of another character, 人 is written 亻. Learners call it the "person radical". You can see it in 你 (nǐ, you), 他 (tā, he) and 们 (men, the plural ending for people).
Compare 大 (dà, big), which began as a person seen from the front.

quiz.explain: 人 means person.
人 is rén, second tone (rising).

quiz.q: How many strokes does 人 have?
quiz.explain: 人 has 2 strokes: one falling left, then one falling right.
大 is big, so 大人 is literally "big person": an adult.

quiz.q: Which shape is the form of 人 used on the left side of characters such as 你 (you)?
quiz.explain: 亻 is the form of 人 used on the left of many characters about people.

sources.name: Make Me a Hanzi / hanzi-writer-data 2.0.1 (stroke data)

characters.summary: 口 (kǒu) is the Chinese character for mouth. It is written with 3 strokes and pronounced kǒu in the third tone. It began as a picture of an open mouth, and you will meet it in everyday words such as 出口 (exit) and 人口 (population).
origin: 口 is a pictograph: it resembles an open mouth.
Today it is a plain box written with three strokes. Besides the mouth itself, it is used for openings of all kinds, such as doorways, exits and entrances.
characters.memory_aid: Picture a mouth opened wide into a square, as if saying "ah".
characters.stroke_order: Three strokes: the left side first, then the top and right side in one stroke, then the bottom line to close the box.
notes: As a small part on the left of other characters, 口 often marks things done with the mouth: 吃 (chī, to eat), 喝 (hē, to drink), 叫 (jiào, to call).
In everyday speech the usual word for a person's mouth is 嘴 (zuǐ). 口 is found mostly inside longer words.

quiz.explain: 口 means mouth.
口 is kǒu, third tone.

quiz.q: How many strokes does 口 have?
quiz.explain: 口 has 3 strokes. The top and right side are written as one stroke.
出 is to go out, so 出口 is the exit.

quiz.q: Which stroke of 口 is written last?
quiz.explain: The bottom line closes the box, so it comes last.

sources.name: Make Me a Hanzi / hanzi-writer-data 2.0.1 (stroke data)

characters.summary: 目 (mù) is the Chinese character for eye. It is written with 5 strokes and pronounced mù in the fourth tone. It began as a picture of an eye, later turned upright, and you will meet it in everyday words such as 目标 (goal) and 节目 (program).
origin: 目 is a pictograph of a human eye. The oldest forms, on oracle bones more than 3,000 years ago, lie on their side, the way an eye really looks: the outline of the eye with the middle of the eye marked inside.
Later the whole shape was rotated 90 degrees and its curves were straightened. That gives the tall box with two lines inside that is written today.
characters.memory_aid: Tilt your head to one side and the character looks like an eye again: the box is the outline of the eye and the two inner lines are the edges of the iris. The video shows this turn.
characters.stroke_order: Five strokes: the left side, then the top and right side in one stroke, then the two short lines inside from top to bottom, and last the bottom line to close the box.
notes: In modern speech the everyday word for eye is 眼睛 (yǎnjing). 目 lives on inside words such as 目标 (goal) and 节目 (program), and as a part of characters about seeing, such as 看 (kàn, to look) and 眼 (yǎn, eye).
Do not mix it up with 日 (rì, sun), which has only one line inside, or with 木 (mù, tree), which sounds exactly the same.

quiz.explain: 目 means eye.
目 is mù, fourth tone (falling).

quiz.q: How many strokes does 目 have?
quiz.explain: 目 has 5 strokes: the box takes three, and there are two lines inside.

quiz.q: How did the old picture of an eye change to become 目?
quiz.explain: The old sideways eye was rotated 90 degrees and its curves became straight lines.
目标 is a goal or target.

sources.name: Make Me a Hanzi / hanzi-writer-data 2.0.1 (stroke data)

characters.summary: 手 (shǒu) is the Chinese character for hand. It is written with 4 strokes and pronounced shǒu in the third tone. It began as a picture of a hand with five fingers, and you will meet it in everyday words such as 手机 (mobile phone) and 洗手 (wash your hands).
origin: 手 is a pictograph of a hand and its fingers. Among the old characters that show hands and claws, this is the one that has always been drawn with five fingers.
In the modern character the top stroke is the middle finger, bent over, and each of the two horizontal strokes stands for two fingers.
characters.memory_aid: Hold up your hand: the long stroke with the hook is your palm and wrist, and the strokes across it are your fingers. The palm-and-wrist part is our way to remember it; the reference we checked only names the fingers.
characters.stroke_order: Four strokes: the short slanting stroke at the top (written from right to left), then the two horizontal strokes from top to bottom, and last the long vertical stroke with a hook.
notes: On the left side of another character, 手 is written 扌, with three strokes. Learners call it the "hand radical". It marks actions done with the hands, as in 打 (dǎ, to hit), 找 (zhǎo, to look for) and 拉 (lā, to pull).
The old form shown above is from bronze inscriptions. We found no oracle-bone image of this character in our source for glyph images.

quiz.explain: 手 means hand.
手 is shǒu, third tone.

quiz.q: How many strokes does 手 have?
quiz.explain: 手 has 4 strokes. The long vertical stroke with a hook comes last.
手机 is literally "hand machine": a mobile phone.

quiz.q: Which shape is the form of 手 used on the left side of characters such as 打 (to hit)?
quiz.explain: 扌 is the three-stroke form of 手 used on the left of many characters about actions of the hand.

sources.name: Make Me a Hanzi / hanzi-writer-data 2.0.1 (stroke data)

characters.summary: 心 (xīn) is the Chinese character for heart. It is written with 4 strokes and pronounced xīn in the first tone. It began as a picture of the heart, and you will meet it in everyday words such as 开心 (happy) and 小心 (be careful).
origin: 心 is a pictograph of a heart. The oldest forms, on oracle bones more than 3,000 years ago, are an outline drawing of it.
The modern shape is highly stylized: one long curved stroke and three short ones. The outline can no longer be seen directly.
characters.memory_aid: Think of the long curved stroke as the rounded base of the heart and the three short strokes as its sides and top. This is how the video draws it. It is a memory aid, not a documented history of each stroke.
characters.stroke_order: Four strokes, from left to right: the short stroke on the left, then the long curved stroke with its hook, then the two short strokes above it, the middle one first and the right one last.
notes: In Chinese, 心 covers both feeling and attention, so it appears in words about mood and care: 开心 (happy), 小心 (careful), 关心 (to care about).
On the left side of a character it is written 忄, as in 忙 (máng, busy). At the bottom it usually keeps its full shape, as in 想 (xiǎng, to think).

quiz.explain: 心 means heart.
心 is xīn, first tone (high and level).

quiz.q: How many strokes does 心 have?
quiz.explain: 心 has 4 strokes: one long curved stroke and three short ones.
小心 is literally "small heart" and means be careful.

quiz.q: Which shape is the form of 心 used on the left side of characters such as 忙 (busy)?
quiz.explain: 忄 is the form of 心 used on the left side of a character.

sources.name: Make Me a Hanzi / hanzi-writer-data 2.0.1 (stroke data)

characters.summary: 月 (yuè) is the Chinese character for moon and month. It is written with 4 strokes and pronounced yuè in the fourth tone. It began as a picture of a crescent moon, and you will meet it in everyday words such as 月亮 (the moon) and 一月 (January).
origin: 月 is a pictograph of a crescent moon. The oldest forms, on oracle bones more than 3,000 years ago, are a curved crescent.
The same character is used for "month".
characters.memory_aid: Think of the two long strokes as the curved edges of a crescent moon, pulled straight, and the two short lines as marks inside it. This is how the video draws it. It is a way to remember the shape, not a documented history of each stroke.
characters.stroke_order: Four strokes: the long stroke on the left that sweeps down to the left, then the top and right side in one stroke ending in a hook, then the two short lines inside, the upper one first.
notes: The months have no names in Chinese, only numbers: 一月 is January ("month one"), 二月 is February, and so on up to 十二月, December.
Inside some other characters this shape does not stand for the moon. In 有 (yǒu, to have), for example, it began as a piece of meat.

quiz.q: Which two meanings does 月 have?
quiz.explain: 月 means moon, and also month.
月 is yuè, fourth tone (falling).

quiz.q: How many strokes does 月 have?
quiz.explain: 月 has 4 strokes: two long ones and two short lines inside.
Months are numbered, so 一月 ("month one") is January.

quiz.q: What does 下个月 (xià ge yuè) mean?
quiz.explain: 下 means next here, so 下个月 is next month. 上个月 is last month.

sources.name: Make Me a Hanzi / hanzi-writer-data 2.0.1 (stroke data)

characters.summary: 雨 (yǔ) is the Chinese character for rain. It is written with 8 strokes and pronounced yǔ in the third tone. It began as a picture of a cloud with raindrops falling from it, and you will meet it in everyday words such as 下雨 (to rain) and 雨伞 (umbrella).
origin: 雨 is a pictograph: a cloud with drops of rain falling from it.
The horizontal stroke at the very top was not part of the original picture. It was added later.
characters.memory_aid: Think of the frame as the cloud and the four dots as raindrops falling from it.
characters.stroke_order: Eight strokes: the horizontal line at the top, the short vertical on the left, the top and right side of the frame in one stroke with a hook, the vertical line down the middle, and then the four dots, the two on the left first and then the two on the right.
notes: On top of other characters 雨 is flattened and marks weather words: 雪 (xuě, snow), 雷 (léi, thunder), 雾 (wù, fog).
Chinese says that rain "comes down": 下雨 (xià yǔ) means it is raining.

quiz.explain: 雨 means rain.
雨 is yǔ, third tone.

quiz.q: How many strokes does 雨 have?
quiz.explain: 雨 has 8 strokes: four for the top line, the frame and the middle line, and four dots.

quiz.q: Which part of 雨 was added later and was not in the original picture?
options: the horizontal stroke at the top
quiz.explain: The original picture was a cloud with falling drops. The top horizontal stroke was added later.
大 is big, so 大雨 is heavy rain.

sources.name: Make Me a Hanzi / hanzi-writer-data 2.0.1 (stroke data)

characters.summary: 云 (yún) is the Chinese character for cloud. It is written with 4 strokes and pronounced yún in the second tone. It began as a simple picture of clouds, and you will meet it in everyday words such as 白云 (white cloud) and 多云 (cloudy).
origin: 云 is a pictograph: a stylized picture of clouds.
Later 雨 (yǔ, rain) was added on top, giving 雲, the form still used in traditional Chinese writing.
The simplified characters adopted in mainland China in the 1950s removed that later addition again, so the modern simplified form is also the older shape.
characters.memory_aid: Think of the two horizontal lines as layers of cloud and the shape below as a curling wisp. This is how the video draws it. It is a memory aid, not a documented history of each stroke.
characters.stroke_order: Four strokes: the short horizontal line, the long horizontal line, then the stroke that goes down to the left and turns back to the right, and last the dot.
notes: Traditional Chinese (Taiwan, Hong Kong) writes 雲, with 12 strokes.
In classical Chinese texts 云 often means "to say".

words.en: Yunnan, a province in south-west China

quiz.explain: 云 means cloud.
云 is yún, second tone (rising).

quiz.q: How many strokes does 云 have?
quiz.explain: 云 has 4 strokes: two horizontal lines, a turning stroke and a dot.

quiz.q: Which character sits on top of the traditional form 雲?
quiz.explain: 雲 is 雨 (rain) on top of 云. The simplified form dropped the 雨 again.
多 is many, so 多云 ("many clouds") means cloudy.

sources.name: Make Me a Hanzi / hanzi-writer-data 2.0.1 (stroke data)

characters.summary: 土 (tǔ) is the Chinese character for earth and soil. It is written with 3 strokes and pronounced tǔ in the third tone. It began as a picture of a mound of earth, and you will meet it in everyday words such as 土地 (land) and 土豆 (potato).
origin: 土 is a pictograph of a mound of earth. The oldest forms are found on oracle bones more than 3,000 years ago.
Later the mound became narrow and pointed at both ends, and its broad middle part developed into the horizontal stroke.
characters.memory_aid: Read it from the bottom up: the long line is the ground, the upright stroke is the mound of earth, and the short line is its wide middle.
characters.stroke_order: Three strokes: the short horizontal line, then the vertical line, then the long horizontal line at the bottom.
notes: Do not confuse 土 with 士 (shì, scholar; soldier). In 土 the bottom line is the longer one. In 士 the top line is longer.
On the left side of other characters it is the "earth radical", as in 地 (dì, ground) and 城 (chéng, city).

quiz.explain: 土 means earth or soil.
土 is tǔ, third tone.

quiz.q: How many strokes does 土 have?
quiz.explain: 土 has 3 strokes: short horizontal, vertical, long horizontal.
土豆 is literally "earth bean": a potato.

quiz.q: In 土, which horizontal line is longer?
options: there is only one horizontal line
quiz.explain: In 土 the bottom line is longer. If the top line is longer, it is a different character, 士.

sources.name: Make Me a Hanzi / hanzi-writer-data 2.0.1 (stroke data)

characters.summary: 田 (tián) is the Chinese character for field. It is written with 5 strokes and pronounced tián in the second tone. It began as a picture of a field divided into sections, and you will meet it in everyday words such as 稻田 (rice field) and 田野 (open fields).
origin: 田 is a pictograph: a field divided into four sections. The form is found on oracle bones more than 3,000 years ago and is still easy to recognise today.
characters.memory_aid: Look down from a hill: a square plot of farmland, with two paths crossing in the middle.
characters.stroke_order: Five strokes: the left side, then the top and right side in one stroke, then the horizontal line inside, then the vertical line inside, and last the bottom line to close the box.
notes: 田 is also a Chinese family name (Tián), and it is a very common part of Japanese family names.
Inside other characters the same square is not always a field. In 果 (guǒ, fruit), for example, it has nothing to do with fields.

quiz.explain: 田 means field.
田 is tián, second tone (rising).

quiz.q: How many strokes does 田 have?
quiz.explain: 田 has 5 strokes: three for the box and two for the cross inside.

quiz.q: What did the original picture show?
options: a field divided into four sections
a box with a cross on the lid
quiz.explain: 田 is a picture of a field divided into four sections.
稻 is the rice plant, so 稻田 is a rice field.

sources.name: Make Me a Hanzi / hanzi-writer-data 2.0.1 (stroke data)

characters.summary: 大 (dà) is the Chinese character for big. It is written with 3 strokes and pronounced dà in the fourth tone. It began as a picture of a person standing and facing forward, and you will meet it in everyday words such as 大家 (everyone) and 大学 (university).
origin: 大 is a pictograph: a standing person facing forward. Compare 人 (rén, person), which shows a person from the side.
It is often explained as a person stretching out the arms to show "big". The oldest forms do not actually show stretched arms, so we give that only as a memory aid.
characters.memory_aid: Stand with your arms and legs spread as wide as you can to show how big something is. That is the shape of 大.
characters.stroke_order: Three strokes: the horizontal line first, then the long stroke that starts at the top, crosses the line and sweeps down to the left, then the stroke that sweeps down to the right.
notes: One more stroke changes the meaning: 太 (tài, too; extremely) has a dot at the bottom, and 天 (tiān, sky; day) has a line on top.
Its opposite is 小 (xiǎo, small). Together they make 大小 (dàxiǎo), size.

quiz.explain: 大 means big.
大 is dà, fourth tone (falling).

quiz.q: How many strokes does 大 have?
quiz.explain: 大 has 3 strokes. The horizontal line is written first.
大学 is literally "big learning": a university.

quiz.q: Which character is 大 with a dot added at the bottom, meaning "too; extremely"?
quiz.explain: 太 (tài) is 大 plus a dot. 天 (tiān, sky) has a line on top instead.

sources.name: Make Me a Hanzi / hanzi-writer-data 2.0.1 (stroke data)

characters.summary: 小 (xiǎo) is the Chinese character for small. It is written with 3 strokes and pronounced xiǎo in the third tone. Its oldest form is three small dots, and you will meet it in everyday words such as 小心 (be careful) and 小时 (hour).
origin: The oldest forms of 小, on oracle bones more than 3,000 years ago, are simply three small dots. There are two readings of them: three tiny dots as a sign for "small", or three grains of sand.
Starting with some bronze inscriptions the dots were drawn longer, which led to the three strokes written today.
An early dictionary, the Shuowen, explained the character as a small object being divided. That explanation was based on the later, stretched shape and is considered a mistake.
characters.memory_aid: Three tiny specks, one in the middle and one on each side. In the modern shape the middle one has grown into a tall stroke with a hook.
characters.stroke_order: Three strokes: the tall vertical stroke with a hook in the middle first, then the dot on the left, then the dot on the right.
notes: Its opposite is 大 (dà, big). Together they make 大小 (dàxiǎo), size.
少 (shǎo, few) looks similar. Compare the two carefully: 少 has one more stroke, sweeping down to the left at the bottom.

quiz.explain: 小 means small.
小 is xiǎo, third tone.

quiz.q: How many strokes does 小 have?
quiz.explain: 小 has 3 strokes.

quiz.q: What did the oldest form of 小 look like?
quiz.explain: The oldest forms are three small dots, read either as a sign for "small" or as grains of sand.

quiz.q: Which stroke of 小 is written first?
options: the tall stroke in the middle
quiz.explain: The tall middle stroke with a hook comes first, then the left dot, then the right dot.

characters.summary: 上 (shàng) is the Chinese character for up and above. It is written with 3 strokes and pronounced shàng in the fourth tone. It began as a sign: a short mark above a long line, and you will meet it in everyday words such as 上午 (morning) and 上山 (go up the mountain).
origin: 上 is not a picture of a thing. It is an indicative sign. The oldest forms, on oracle bones more than 3,000 years ago, are a short line drawn above a long curved line, to show the idea of "above".
下 (xià, below) was made the same way, with the short line under the long one.
In the modern form an upright stroke stands on the base line, with the short line on its right.
characters.memory_aid: The long line at the bottom is the ground. Everything else in the character stands above it.
characters.stroke_order: Three strokes: the vertical line first, then the short horizontal line on its right, then the long horizontal line at the bottom.
notes: 上 is also a verb, to go up or to get on: 上山 (go up the mountain), 上车 (get on a vehicle), 上班 (go to work).
With time words it means "last": 上个月 (last month), 上次 (last time).

quiz.explain: 上 means up or above.
上 is shàng, fourth tone (falling).

quiz.q: How many strokes does 上 have?
quiz.explain: 上 has 3 strokes: vertical, short horizontal, long horizontal.

quiz.q: What did the oldest form of 上 show?
options: a short mark above a long line
quiz.explain: It is a sign, not a picture: a short mark above a long line.
上午 is the part of the day before noon: the morning.

characters.summary: 下 (xià) is the Chinese character for down and below. It is written with 3 strokes and pronounced xià in the fourth tone. It began as a sign: a short mark below a long line, and you will meet it in everyday words such as 下午 (afternoon) and 下雨 (to rain).
origin: 下 is not a picture of a thing. It is an indicative sign. The oldest forms, on oracle bones more than 3,000 years ago, are a short line drawn below a long curved line, to show the idea of "below".
上 (shàng, above) was made the same way, with the short line over the long one.
In the modern form an upright stroke hangs down from the long line, with a dot on its right.
characters.memory_aid: The long line at the top is the ground seen from the side. Everything else in the character hangs below it.
characters.stroke_order: Three strokes: the horizontal line at the top, then the vertical line, then the dot on the right.
notes: 下 is also a verb, to go down or to get off: 下山 (go down the mountain), 下车 (get off a vehicle), 下班 (finish work). Rain and snow "come down" too: 下雨 (to rain), 下雪 (to snow).
With time words it means "next": 下个月 (next month), 下次 (next time).

quiz.explain: 下 means down or below.
下 is xià, fourth tone (falling).

quiz.q: How many strokes does 下 have?
quiz.explain: 下 has 3 strokes: horizontal, vertical, dot.
下午 is the part of the day after noon: the afternoon.

quiz.q: What does 下个月 (xià ge yuè) mean?
quiz.explain: With time words 下 means next, so 下个月 is next month.

characters.summary: 中 (zhōng) is the Chinese character for middle. It is written with 4 strokes and pronounced zhōng in the first tone. It began as a picture of a flagpole, and you will meet it in everyday words such as 中国 (China) and 中午 (noon).
origin: 中 is a pictograph of a flagpole. The oldest forms, on oracle bones more than 3,000 years ago, show an upright pole with streamers and a rounded shape at its middle.

Based on archaeological evidence, the shape in the middle has been interpreted as a drum fixed to the pole. A pole like this was placed in the centre of a field to gather people and to show the direction of the wind.
Other explanations exist. The Shuowen, an early dictionary, read the character as a line passing through the centre of 口, and it has also been explained as an arrow in the centre of a target.
characters.memory_aid: A line straight through the middle of a box. This is the easiest way to remember the modern shape.
characters.stroke_order: Four strokes: the short left side of the box, then its top and right side in one stroke, then the bottom line of the box, and last the long vertical line through the middle.
notes: 中国 (Zhōngguó), the Chinese name for China, is literally "middle country".
Pronounced zhòng, in the fourth tone, the same character is a verb meaning to hit a target, as in 中奖 (zhòngjiǎng, to win a prize).

quiz.explain: 中 means middle.

quiz.q: How is 中 pronounced when it means middle?
quiz.explain: 中 is zhōng, first tone (high and level).

quiz.q: How many strokes does 中 have?
quiz.explain: 中 has 4 strokes: three for the box, then the long vertical line.

quiz.q: What is 中国 (Zhōngguó), literally "middle country"?
quiz.explain: 中国 is the Chinese name for China.

quiz.q: Which stroke of 中 is written last?
options: the left side of the box
the bottom line of the box
the long vertical line through the middle
quiz.explain: The box is written first. The long vertical line through the middle comes last.

characters.summary: 黄 (huáng) is the Chinese character for yellow. It is written with 11 strokes and pronounced huáng in the second tone. It is also a very common family name, and you will meet it in words such as 黄色 (yellow) and 黄河 (the Yellow River).
origin: The origin of 黄 is debated. The oldest forms, on oracle bones more than 3,000 years ago, show a standing person with a ring or box shape drawn at the waist.

One proposal is that this was a picture of a person wearing a jade pendant, and that it was the first way of writing 璜 (huáng, a jade pendant). Another reads the same forms as a person with a swollen belly. Scholars do not agree, so we do not give either as fact.
What is certain is that the character was already being used for the colour yellow in the oracle-bone inscriptions, and that is the meaning that lasted.
characters.memory_aid: Think of the middle box 由 as a field of ripe yellow grain, with grass growing on top and two roots below. This is only a way to remember the modern shape. It is not where the character comes from.
characters.stroke_order: Start at the top: a horizontal stroke, two short vertical strokes through it, then the long horizontal stroke. Next write the box in the middle (left side, then top and right side in one stroke, the inner horizontal, the vertical through the centre, and the closing stroke). Finish with the two strokes at the bottom, left then right.
notes: 黄 is also one of the most common Chinese family names. In Mandarin it is spelled Huang. Families from Cantonese-speaking areas often spell the same character Wong.
The form 黄 is used in mainland China, Singapore and Japan. In traditional Chinese writing (Taiwan, Hong Kong) the character is written 黃, with one more stroke.

quiz.explain: 黄 means yellow.
黄 is huáng, second tone (rising).

quiz.q: How many strokes does 黄 have in its simplified form?
quiz.explain: 黄 has 11 strokes. The traditional form 黃 has 12.
河 is river, so 黄河 is the Yellow River.
黄瓜 is cucumber, even though the name is literally "yellow melon".
